name: Operations in the District AI Policy
title: Operations in the District AI Policy
answer: A district AI policy should cover operations tools, not just classroom tools, because operations decisions such as bus routes and meal portions affect students every day. The same principles of privacy, human review, and verified results should apply to these tools. A simple inventory of operations AI helps a district see where those protections exist and where they are missing.

sections.body: District AI policies tend to concentrate on classrooms and leave operations out, even though operations tools make daily decisions that touch students, from how buses are routed to how much food is served. The idea is that an operations tool using AI should be held to the same standards as any classroom tool: privacy, human review, and verified results. The problem it solves is the blind spot that appears when a district believes it has an AI policy but has never examined the systems running behind transportation, facilities, and finance. A sound policy, as described earlier in the book, supplies the elements to apply here. Bringing operations into the policy closes the gap between what the district says it governs and what it actually governs.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, the work starts with a simple inventory. The district lists every operations tool that uses AI, the decisions each one supports, who reviews its output, and what data it uses. That list makes visible where human review and privacy protections are already in place and where they are absent. It also gives the board a clear picture of how AI is being used in operations. The text does not give grade band examples for this idea, because the subject is district-level operations rather than classroom practice.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study or finding on the effectiveness of this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it does provide is legal context. Texas's AI governance law defines covered government entities broadly enough to include school districts, and it took effect in January 2026 (Texas Legislature, 2025). Ohio requires every district to adopt an AI policy, and its state model policy is available to guide districts (Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, 2026). The book advises districts to confirm their obligations with counsel.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about scope and responsibility. State laws may apply to operations tools as well as classroom ones, and districts are told to confirm their obligations with counsel rather than assume. The inventory is a tool for oversight, not a substitute for it, and it exists to reveal where human review and privacy protections are missing. Decisions about what to do with what the inventory shows remain with people, including the board, which receives the picture of AI in operations. Nothing in the text removes the need for human review of the outputs these tools produce.
